title: Maunalua Bay Beach Ohana 28 v. State
description: Whether the circuit court erred in awarding zero dollars in just compensation for the temporary taking of accreted lands and in denying attorneys' fees under the private attorney general doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The Ohanas argued they were entitled to more than zero dollars in just compensation (including nominal damages) for the temporary taking of their accreted lands and to attorneys' fees under the private attorney general doctrine for vindicating constitutional rights and causing the repeal of an unconstitutional statute.
defendant_argument: The State of Hawai'i argued that zero dollars was appropriate just compensation because the accreted land had no fair market rental value, and that attorneys' fees were barred by sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Hawaii affirmed the circuit court's decision, holding that zero dollars was the correct amount for just compensation for the temporary taking and that attorneys' fees were barred by sovereign immunity.

title: State v. Spies
description: Whether Spies's conviction should be vacated due to insufficient foundation for scientific drug test results and unlawful detention leading to inadmissible incriminating statements.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Intermediate Court of Appeals (ICA) erred in vacating the conviction, asserting that sufficient foundation was laid for expert testimony and that Spies's detention and statements were lawful.
defendant_argument: Spies argued that the ICA correctly vacated his conviction due to insufficient foundation for the drug test results and that his detention was unlawful, making his incriminating statements inadmissible.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the ICA's judgment and affirmed Spies's conviction, finding that the State laid a proper foundation for the expert testimony and that Spies's detention and initial incriminating statement were lawful, while subsequent statements, though obtained in violation of Miranda, were harmless error.

title: Winn v. Brady
description: Whether a recorded judgment lien constitutes a constitutionally protected property interest requiring personal notice for junior lienholders before an execution sale, and whether this new rule should apply retroactively or prospectively.
plaintiff_argument: The Winn parties, as junior judgment lienholders, held a constitutionally protected property interest and were deprived of due process when their lien was extinguished without personal or actual notice of the execution sale, as notice by publication was insufficient.
defendant_argument: The Spences argued that the execution sale was not a state action, thus not implicating due process rights, and that a judgment lien does not create a protected property interest. They contended that notice by publication, as per HRS § 651-43, was sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that a junior judgment lienholder with a recorded judgment is entitled to constitutional due process notice, including personal notice for the Winn parties. However, the court reversed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' decision to apply this rule to the instant case, holding that the new rule shall apply prospectively only to writs of execution filed after the date of this opinion.

title: Hawaii v. Zuffante
description: Whether the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires law enforcement to record custodial interrogations, both in-station and, when feasible, outside the station, with the plaintiff arguing against such a requirement and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Hawaiʻi argued that existing precedent (Kekona) did not require recording and that current times did not warrant overturning that rule.
defendant_argument: Charles Zuffante argued that the lack of recording undermined his right against self-incrimination and a fair trial, urging the court to adopt a recording requirement.
decision_outcome: The court held that the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires law enforcement to record all in-station custodial interrogations and, when feasible, all outside-the-station custodial interrogations, overruling State v. Kekona. The lower court's judgment and sentence against Zuffante were vacated, and the case was remanded.

title: Grube v. Trader; State v. Rogan
description: Whether the circuit court erred in sealing judicial records related to a criminal proceeding and in requiring a reporter to retain counsel to assert his constitutional right of public access to those records.
plaintiff_argument: Grube argued that the circuit court failed to meet the procedural and substantive requirements for sealing records, and that he had a personal constitutional right to represent himself pro se in asserting public access to judicial records.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the circuit court properly identified a compelling interest in preserving ongoing investigations, that the sealing order was narrowly tailored, and that Grube, as a non-attorney, could not represent Civil Beat's interests.
decision_outcome: The court granted Grube's petition for a writ of mandamus, ordering the circuit court to unseal the documents (unless the State requests a hearing to provide additional evidence within ten days) and permitting Grube to represent himself pro se in further proceedings. The court denied the writ of prohibition as unnecessary.

title: Hilo Bay Marina v. State of Hawaii
description: Whether a state deed restriction requiring land use for "church purposes only" violates the Hawaiʻi Constitution's Establishment Clause, with the plaintiff arguing it constitutes state action advancing religion and the defendant arguing for alignment with federal First Amendment interpretations allowing more religious accommodation.
plaintiff_argument: The deed restriction requiring land use for "church purposes only" constitutes state action that advances religion and violates Hawaiʻi’s Establishment Clause, which mandates a strict separation of church and state.
defendant_argument: The Hawaiʻi Constitution's Establishment Clause should be interpreted co-extensively with the federal First Amendment, and recent U.S. Supreme Court rulings (like Kennedy) allow for greater accommodation of religion, making the deed restriction permissible.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Circuit Court erred in granting summary judgment to the State and that summary judgment is warranted for Hilo Bay, indicating the deed restriction is a violation of the Establishment Clause.

title: Foresman v. Foresman
description: Whether HRS § 657-1.8(a) violates the ex post facto clause of the U.S. Constitution and whether the Circuit Court should have instructed the jury on criminal statutes in effect at the time of the alleged sexual abuse rather than when the complaint was filed.
plaintiff_argument: HRS § 657-1.8 is constitutional, and any error in jury instructions was harmless because the defendant's admitted conduct would have constituted a criminal offense under statutes in effect at the time of the acts.
defendant_argument: HRS § 657-1.8(a) is unconstitutional as it violates the ex post facto clause by imposing civil liability for acts not criminal when committed, and the Circuit Court erred by using subsequently enacted criminal statutes for jury instructions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, which upheld the Circuit Court's final judgment, finding that while the jury instructions were erroneous, the error was harmless given the defendant's admissions.

title: State v. Hoffman
description: Whether a defendant's un-Mirandized statements, made in response to police words or conduct "normally attendant to arrest and custody," are admissible if those words or conduct were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, thus constituting "interrogation" under the Hawaiʻi State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Hoffman argued that an officer's conduct and statements "normally attendant to arrest and custody" could still constitute interrogation, triggering Miranda warnings, if they were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Hoffman's statements were made in response to Officer Tavares's statements or actions "normally attendant to arrest and custody" and therefore did not constitute "interrogation," making them admissible without Miranda warnings.
decision_outcome: The court vacated in part the ICA's judgment and the circuit court's order, holding that some of Hoffman's un-Mirandized statements were made in response to interrogation and should be suppressed, while others were not and are admissible, based on whether the officer's words or conduct were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.

title: Surface Water Use Permit Applications
description: Whether the Commission on Water Resource Management's decisions regarding instream flow standards and surface water use permits for Nā Wai 'Ehā complied with constitutional and statutory mandates, protected Native Hawaiian rights, and avoided unlawful delegation of authority.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants (MMK, Hui/MTF, OHA, Mahi Pono, WWC) argued that the Commission failed to restore stream flows, did not justify its IIFS decisions, unlawfully delegated public trust duties, and violated due process rights in water allocations.
defendant_argument: The Commission contended that it properly set the IIFS, made reasonable water allocations, did not violate due process rights, and did not unlawfully delegate its authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated and remanded the Commission's decision regarding the Interim Instream Flow Standards (IIFS) and the unlawful delegation of public trust duties, but affirmed the Commission's decisions on MMK's water allocation, Mahi Pono's due process rights, WWC's due process rights, and the Public Utilities Commission's jurisdiction.

title: State v. Tran
description: Whether Hawai'i's statute on continuous sexual assault of a minor and its related constitutional provision violate the U.S. Constitution's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments regarding jury unanimity on specific predicate acts and the sufficiency of the indictment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the circuit court erred in dismissing the indictment, that the Motta/Wells liberal construction standard should apply, and that the state's constitutional and statutory provisions do not violate the U.S. Constitution's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments regarding jury unanimity on specific predicate acts.
defendant_argument: Tran argued that the state's constitutional and statutory provisions are unconstitutional under Ramos v. Louisiana because they permit non-unanimous jury verdicts on specific acts, and that the indictment was insufficiently specific under Jardine, thus violating his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment rights, and should have been dismissed with prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order granting in part and denying in part Tran's motion to dismiss, affirmed the circuit court's denial of Tran's supplemented new trial motion, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Kanahele v. State
description: Whether Act 14 of 1995 precludes claims regarding the 2018 designation of the Mauna Kea Access Road (MKAR) as a state highway, with plaintiffs arguing it does not and defendants arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Act 14 of 1995 does not bar their claims because the 2018 designation of the MKAR as a state highway constituted a new breach of trust, and the State failed to follow proper procedures for this designation, violating its fiduciary duties under the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act (HHCA).
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Act 14 of 1995 fully and finally resolved all claims related to the uncompensated use of Hawaiian home lands for state roads and highways, including the MKAR, and the 2018 designation did not give rise to any new claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the circuit court's summary judgment in favor of the defendants and remanded the case with instructions to grant summary judgment to the plaintiffs.

title: Davis v. Bissen
description: Whether the County of Maui was constitutionally required to provide a contested case hearing before seizing and destroying the personal property of houseless individuals during an encampment sweep.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that their personal property, including items used for shelter and survival, constituted a protected property interest under the state and federal constitutions, requiring a pre-deprivation contested case hearing before seizure and destruction.
defendant_argument: The County argued that houseless individuals had no protected property interest in storing belongings on public land, and even if they did, existing procedures like notice and outreach were sufficient, making a contested case hearing unnecessary and administratively burdensome.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's order, holding that the Hawai'i Constitution's due process clause required a pre-deprivation contested case hearing for plaintiffs Davis and Lau before their personal property could be seized and destroyed, and thus properly denied the County's motion to dismiss as to them.

title: State v. Wilson
description: Whether Hawaiʻi's 'place to keep' laws (HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a)) violate an individual's right to keep and bear arms for self-defense under the Hawaiʻi Constitution and the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Wilson lacked standing to challenge the licensing law and that the 'place to keep' laws do not violate constitutional rights, as Hawaiʻi has no state constitutional right to carry a firearm in public and the Second Amendment allows for restrictions.
defendant_argument: Wilson argued that HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a) infringe upon his constitutional right to keep and bear a firearm for self-defense, citing Bruen and claiming both the U.S. and Hawaiʻi Constitutions confer this right to carry a handgun for self-defense outside the home.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order granting the defendant's motion to dismiss counts 1 and 2 and remanded the case to the Circuit Court of the Second Circuit.

title: State v. Lafoga
description: Whether the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, without strong justification and without taking precautions to mitigate prejudice, violated the defendants' constitutional rights to a fair trial, presumption of innocence, impartial jury, and effective assistance of counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The State implicitly argued that the anonymous jury was permissible or that any error in empaneling it was harmless, and that the court took reasonable precautions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the anonymous jury violated their constitutional rights to presumption of innocence, an impartial jury, effective assistance of counsel, and an impartial tribunal, constituting structural error requiring a new trial.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, concluding that any error was harmless.

title: State v. Hewitt
description: Whether Miranda warnings are required for police questioning of a person confined to a hospital bed, specifically regarding when "custody" is established under the Hawai'i Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing warnings were not required and the defendant arguing they were.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Hewitt was not in custody at the time of questioning, and therefore, Miranda warnings were not required.
defendant_argument: Hewitt argued that she was in custody during police questioning in the hospital and was thus entitled to Miranda warnings.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the ICA's judgment, affirmed the district court's judgment of nolle prosequi for both counts against Hewitt, expressly overruled *Sagapolutele-Silva*'s abrogation of *Ketchum*'s bright-line rule, and held that Miranda warnings are required when probable cause to arrest has developed or when a person is in custody under the totality of circumstances.

title: Ohana v. Univiversity of Hawai'i
description: Whether the burden of proof shifts to the government in constitutional challenges to administrative rules based on Article XII, Section 7 of the Hawai'i Constitution, and what standard governs such challenges.
plaintiff_argument: The Flores-Case 'Ohana (FCO) argued that the burden of proof should shift to the government and that the Ka Pa'akai framework, which requires agencies to consider the impact on Native Hawaiian rights, should apply to administrative rulemaking.
defendant_argument: The University of Hawai'i (UH) promulgated the rules. The Attorney General (amicus curiae) argued that the burden of proof should remain with the challenging party and that the Ka Pa'akai framework, designed for contested cases, should not apply in the same way to administrative rulemaking because rulemaking does not produce an evidentiary record.
decision_outcome: The court held that the burden of proof remains with the challenging party, but affirmed that the Ka Pa'akai framework applies to administrative rulemaking, requiring agencies to conduct a contemporaneous analysis of Native Hawaiian traditional and customary rights before adopting rules. The case was remanded for further proceedings.

title: State v. Canosa
description: Whether a sixteen-month delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and a fundamentally fair sentencing proceeding, and whether this delay rendered the defendant's allocution constitutionally inadequate.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the delay did not prevent the court from legally resentencing the defendant, nor did it constitute a waiver of the State's right, and that the defendant's claims were waived.
defendant_argument: Canosa argued that the sixteen-month delay in sentencing violated his due process rights and right to allocution, especially because the ordinary maximum terms of imprisonment had expired before resentencing, making the extended sentences illegal.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, ruling that the State's unreasonable delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and a fundamentally fair sentencing proceeding, and ordered his immediate release with a sentence of time served.

title: State v. Obrero
description: Whether Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (HRS) § 801-1, which requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions, was implicitly repealed or superseded by a 1982 constitutional amendment allowing felony charges via preliminary hearing.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the 1982 constitutional amendment to Article I, Section 10, effectively nullified HRS § 801-1's grand jury protections by authorizing the State to use complaints and preliminary hearings to initiate felony prosecutions, and that HRS § 801-1 was implicitly repealed.
defendant_argument: Obrero argued that HRS § 801-1 plainly requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions not within district court jurisdiction or chargeable by information, that the statute has not been implicitly repealed, and that the State's use of a preliminary hearing after a grand jury no-bill is unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's denial of Obrero's motion to dismiss, ruling that the State cannot subject Obrero to trial and sentencing without a grand jury indictment as required by HRS § 801-1.

title: State v. Sagapolutele-Silva
description: Whether the test for determining if a suspect is "in custody" for Miranda warnings should rely solely on the existence of probable cause (as argued by lower courts and implicitly supported by the defendant's initial success) or on a totality of the circumstances (as argued by the State and ultimately adopted by the Supreme Court).
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the "custody" test for Miranda warnings should be based on the totality of the circumstances, with probable cause being relevant but not dispositive.
defendant_argument: Sagapolutele-Silva argued that, even under a totality of the circumstances test, she was in custody during the OVUII investigation, and the lower courts had correctly suppressed her statements based on probable cause.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the lower court's order suppressing Sagapolutele-Silva's statements, clarifying that custody is determined by the totality of the circumstances, not solely by probable cause, and remanded the case.

title: Hicks v. 2021 Hawaii Reapportionment Commission
description: Whether the 2021 Hawaiʻi Reapportionment Commission was required to fully implement the 'district within district' guidelines for legislative districts, or if it had discretion to consider them alongside other policy objectives.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the 2021 Reapportionment Plan is invalid because it fails to give adequate effect to constitutional and statutory 'district within district' guidelines, which require representative districts to be wholly included within senatorial districts and legislative districts within U.S. congressional districts, even when practicable.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that it satisfied its obligations by considering the 'district within district' guidelines alongside other policy objectives and that the guidelines are discretionary, not mandatory, thus the Plan is valid and no abuse of discretion occurred.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request, ruling that the Reapportionment Commission has discretion in applying 'district within district' guidelines and is not required to give them any particular effect, as long as they are considered.

title: League of Women Voters of Honolulu  v. State
description: Whether a bill that undergoes a non-germane amendment must restart the constitutional three readings process in each legislative house.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Act 84 was unconstitutional because the bill's substance was entirely changed by a non-germane amendment, requiring new readings in the Senate, which did not occur.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the Legislature's rules permit a bill to be read by title only and do not require new readings after amendments, even if the content is entirely substituted.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's summary judgment for the State and remanded the case with instructions to grant the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, ruling Act 84 invalid.

title: In re Individuals in Custody of the State
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Hawaii should grant extraordinary relief to order the expedited release of certain inmates and mandate specific public health measures in correctional facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, or if existing legal mechanisms and changed circumstances render such relief unnecessary.
plaintiff_argument: The Office of the Public Defender (OPD) argued that the COVID-19 pandemic created an unprecedented public health emergency requiring extraordinary relief, including the expedited release of certain categories of inmates and court-ordered public health measures in correctional facilities, to protect inmates and the public.
defendant_argument: The respondents (DPS, prosecuting attorneys) argued that conditions had changed since prior petitions, with widespread vaccine availability and a federal settlement addressing pandemic response in correctional facilities, making the requested extraordinary relief unwarranted and that existing legal mechanisms for inmate release were sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition in part, ordering the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to comply with HRS § 353-6.2 regarding periodic reviews and transmission of findings for pretrial detainees, but denied all other requests for extraordinary relief.

title: State v. Lee
description: Whether evidence obtained after police entered Joshua Lee's bedroom without a warrant, responding to a suicide call, should be suppressed under the "fruit of the poisonous tree" doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The evidence should be suppressed because the police entry was an unlawful warrantless search, and the emergency aid exception does not apply under the Hawai'i Constitution.
defendant_argument: The evidence should not be suppressed because the entry was justified by an emergency aid exception or, alternatively, Lee's subsequent actions constituted new crimes that severed any causal link to the initial entry.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, vacating the circuit court's order to suppress evidence, but on different grounds, ruling that the evidence was not "fruit of the poisonous tree."
